content.comment_body: Hello, It would be useful to collect unresolved bugs and misconceptions in one place to prevent repeated mistakes. I noticed after writing complex math routines that reopening the program in the simulator sometimes produces incorrect results. The issue seems to be related to using separate links and not collapsing parameter boxes; values for some links don't update unless you collapse and expand all parameter boxes. This topic was discussed in previous years, but isn't mentioned in help files. Also, I was surprised by calculation results like 180/360=1, but that's on me for not reading the documentation carefully.
I'm unclear about which 'bugs' you are referring to.

I'm referring to programming problems, often due to unclear explanations in manuals. The issue with separated links is that some values update and some don't, depending on the function block used. There is also no clear distinction between the simulator and actual PLC—testing is needed. Debugging on a large local network is slow since the software scans all devices, taking up to 5 minutes, and the network card/IP selection only becomes available afterwards. Additionally, the internal math function block uses fractions and 32-bit integers, which isn't explained.

I haven't encountered this issue before. I agree that simulation isn't the same as real device operation. For me, these problems haven't occurred. As for the mathematical instructions, I'm unsure if they use fractions, floats, or integers internally, and it's true the manuals don't explain this. But I don't know of any PLC manual from any manufacturer that explains every detail one hundred percent.

The main idea is to compile useful knowledge not documented officially, to help others avoid repeated mistakes. For example: Math instructions are executed in block number order, so if blocks are arranged in reverse and enabled only for one cycle, you might get old values. This can be used for creating an analog value shift register. Also, virtual memory can overlap. A centralized wiki could make this information more accessible, helping users avoid common pitfalls.

Who actually reads and posts in such threads? Very few people. The latest product version has been available for months, but questions about connecting to the new model still come up frequently. I've answered many times that a certain software version is required, but this wouldn't be necessary if users used the forum search function.

I faced a similar issue at work when someone suggested a directory for troubleshooting a recurring issue. My response was that it doesn't matter where the solution is stored if no one reads it. That's just how things are in practice.

You are both correct. There is a bias where some users ask questions without searching first, while others find answers on their own and never post. Threads about software versions show high engagement. However, searching for answers in this forum is difficult—the forum system itself is outdated. Improving information accessibility here would be challenging; a dedicated wiki platform might help. The real challenge would be finding volunteers willing to invest time in building and maintaining a useful knowledge base.

analysis.insight_summary: Users have ongoing issues with mathematical logic in the simulator—incorrect values arise unless specific interface actions are taken, and documentation isn't clear on why. There are notable differences between simulation and real device execution, with little official explanation of internal math block operations. Programming across large networks is also hampered by slow device discovery. Overall, frustration stems from ambiguous system behavior documentation and the lack of centralized resources for collecting known issues.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect dependable simulation and programming tools, comprehensive documentation on differences between simulation and real hardware operation, transparency about internal workings of math blocks, more efficient management for large networks, and easier access to information about known problems.
